Confidence Interval for the Ratio of Two Independent Means

Source: R/ci_ratio_of_means.R
ci_ratio_of_means.Rd

Computes a confidence set for the ratio of two population means estimated from independent groups, \(\rho = \mu_1 / \mu_2\), or, with a third, baseline group, for the ratio of the two groups' advantages over the baseline, \(\rho = (\mu_1 - \mu_b) / (\mu_2 - \mu_b)\). A ratio states an effect in relative terms (a new procedure's mean is 90 percent of the standard procedure's), which is the natural scale when the outcome has a meaningful zero. The second form is the fraction of a reference treatment's advantage over a placebo or a trivial baseline that a new treatment retains, the retention of effect of the three-arm noninferiority trial (Pigeot et al., 2003). The default interval is Fieller's, which inverts the t test of \(\mu_1 - \rho \mu_2 = 0\) and is reported as what it is: a bounded interval, the complement of an interval, or the whole line. The log-scale interval of the response ratio and percentile and BCa bootstrap intervals are offered beside it. For two means measured on the same units, see ci_ratio_of_means_paired.

Usage

ci_ratio_of_means(
  x = NULL,
  y = NULL,
  baseline = NULL,
  mean_1 = NULL,
  sd_1 = NULL,
  n_1 = NULL,
  mean_2 = NULL,
  sd_2 = NULL,
  n_2 = NULL,
  mean_baseline = NULL,
  sd_baseline = NULL,
  n_baseline = NULL,
  var_equal = FALSE,
  ci_method = c("fieller", "log", "percentile", "bca"),
  conf_level = 0.95,
  alpha_lower = NULL,
  alpha_upper = NULL,
  B = 10000L,
  seed = NULL
)

Arguments

x, y

Numeric vectors of observations from the numerator group and the denominator group. The groups are independent and need not be the same size; NAs are removed from each vector separately.

baseline

An optional numeric vector of observations from a third, independent baseline group (a placebo arm, a trivial comparison condition). When it is supplied the ratio is that of the advantages, \((\mu_1 - \mu_b) / (\mu_2 - \mu_b)\).

mean_1, mean_2

Group sample means, for analysis from summary statistics in place of x and y.

sd_1, sd_2

Group sample standard deviations (with \(n - 1\) in the denominator of the variance).

n_1, n_2

Group sample sizes.

mean_baseline, sd_baseline, n_baseline

The baseline group's sample mean, standard deviation, and size, for the ratio of the two groups' advantages over it from summary statistics (the three arms a noninferiority trial reports). Supply all three or none.

var_equal

Logical. FALSE (the default) lets the group variances differ and inverts the Welch-type test, whose degrees of freedom change with the hypothesized ratio; TRUE pools the variances, which gives Fieller's exact interval under normality and equal variances. Used by "fieller" and "log"; the bootstrap resamples each group from itself and needs neither.

ci_method

The interval: "fieller" (the default), "log" (the response ratio interval, formed on the log scale and defined only when both means, or both advantages, are positive), "percentile", or "bca" (bootstrap intervals, which need the raw data).

conf_level

Confidence level (default 0.95).

alpha_lower

The tail area at the lower limit. An omitted confidence level yields to supplied tail areas; an explicit level must agree with them. Each tail area is at most .5.

alpha_upper

The tail area at the upper limit, supplied together with alpha_lower. The table records the coverage, 1 - alpha_lower - alpha_upper, as its level and, when the two tail areas differ, the areas themselves, which the line beneath the printed table, results_sentence, and the alpha_lower and alpha_upper columns of tidy() state; with a tail area of 0 the interval is a one-sided confidence bound, unbounded on that side.

B

Number of bootstrap replications for "percentile" and "bca", a single whole number (ignored otherwise). Default 10000: a replication of a ratio of means costs little, so a reported interval deserves the default, and the BCa adjustment moves the working quantiles into the tails, where a small B is least stable. The fewest accepted with 0.025 in each tail is 400 for the percentile interval and 2000 for BCa (200 and 1000 at a 0.90 level, 2000 and 10000 at 0.99); with unequal tail areas the smaller one decides. A smaller B is refused before anything is computed (class dmar_count_invalid). See Bootstrap replications under Details and dmar_bootstrap.

seed

Optional integer seed for the bootstrap. The default NULL uses the current state of the random number generator; a supplied seed is set for the call and the prior state restored on exit.

Value

A long data.frame (classes dmar_ci_ratio_of_means, dmar_ci_long, dmar_tbl) with columns term and value, whose rows are ci_lower, ratio, and ci_upper (the set's outer ends, -Inf or Inf when it is unbounded on that side); excluded_lower and excluded_upper (the ends of the excluded gap of a complement or a union of two intervals, NA otherwise); mean_1, mean_2, and mean_baseline (the group means; mean_baseline is NA without a baseline); se_1, se_2, and se_baseline (the standard errors of the means, from the pooled variance when var_equal = TRUE); t_denominator (the denominator, \(\bar x_2\) or \(\bar x_2 - \bar x_b\), over its standard error); df (the degrees of freedom of that t: pooled, or Satterthwaite's for the denominator when var_equal = FALSE); and n_1, n_2, and n_baseline. The rows are the same for every call. Attributes: confidence_set ("interval", "complement of an interval", "whole line", or, with unequal tail areas only, "union of two intervals"; NA when a bootstrap interval was withheld and both limits are NA), ci_method, var_equal, conf_level, and the tail areas when they differ; df_limits when var_equal = FALSE and the interval is Fieller's or the log ratio's, the degrees of freedom of the test at each end of the set, a vector with elements lower, upper, excluded_lower, and excluded_upper that is NA at an end no test decides (an infinite limit, the open end of a one-sided bound, or a gap the set does not have); B, B_used, n_dropped, B_required, and bootstrap_status for a bootstrap interval (see Bootstrap replications under Details); and fieller_set (the form of the Fieller set) when the interval is a log or bootstrap interval and the Fieller set at the same level is unbounded. tidy() returns the ratio, its limits, the ends of any excluded gap, and the form of the set in one row (see dmar_tidiers).

Details

Fieller's confidence set. For a candidate ratio \(\rho\) the contrast \(\bar x_1 - \rho \bar x_2\) (with a baseline, \((\bar x_1 - \bar x_b) - \rho (\bar x_2 - \bar x_b)\)) estimates zero exactly when \(\rho\) is the population ratio, and its t statistic, $$T(\rho) = \frac{\hat\theta_1 - \rho \hat\theta_2} {\sqrt{v_{11} - 2 \rho v_{12} + \rho^2 v_{22}}},$$ where \(\hat\theta_1\) and \(\hat\theta_2\) are the numerator and denominator and the \(v\) terms their estimated variances and covariance, is a pivot: it involves the data and \(\rho\) alone (Fieller, 1941, 1954). The 1941 reference is Fieller's study of the biological standardization of insulin, which Fieller (1954) cites with the year 1940. The confidence set is every \(\rho\) that the test does not reject, the solution of a quadratic inequality in \(\rho\). Its form is decided by the denominator's t, \(\hat\theta_2 / \sqrt{v_{22}}\), reported in the t_denominator row (Fieller, 1954, p. 177). The row keeps the sign of the denominator, and only its absolute value matters: when the absolute value of the denominator's t exceeds the critical value (with unequal tail areas, each side of the estimate is bounded when that absolute value exceeds the side's own critical value) the set is a bounded interval. When it does not, the set contains arbitrarily large values of the ratio, as it should when the data cannot distinguish the denominator from zero: it is then either the complement of an interval, every value outside a gap, or, when the data are consistent with every ratio at the chosen level, the whole line. The table reports all three as they are. The ci_lower and ci_upper rows are the outer ends of the set (-Inf and Inf when it is unbounded), and the excluded_lower and excluded_upper rows are the ends of the gap of a complement (NA otherwise): the set is every value from ci_lower to ci_upper except those strictly between excluded_lower and excluded_upper. The confidence_set attribute names the form, and so does the line printed under the table; results_sentence writes the set in that form, for example as every value except those between the ends of the gap. With unequal tail areas one side of the set can be bounded while the other is not, which can also give an interval unbounded on one side or the union of two intervals. von Luxburg and Franz (2009) derive the same sets geometrically, from confidence intervals for the means of linear combinations of the two variables.

Equal or unequal variances. With var_equal = TRUE the variances are pooled over the groups, on \(n_1 + n_2 - 2\) degrees of freedom (\(n_1 + n_2 + n_b - 3\) with a baseline), and the set is Fieller's exact one under normality and equal variances. With the default var_equal = FALSE each group keeps its own variance and the contrast is tested as Welch's t tests a difference, with Satterthwaite degrees of freedom; those degrees of freedom depend on \(\rho\), so the set has no closed form and is found by solving for the values of \(\rho\) at which the test's p-value equals its tail area. The interval therefore agrees with the test: without a baseline and with equal tail areas, each finite end \(L\) of the set (a limit or an end of the gap) is a value at which t.test(x, L * y) has p-value 1 - conf_level; with a baseline the test is that of the contrast \(\bar x_1 - L \bar x_2 - (1 - L) \bar x_b\), with the Satterthwaite degrees of freedom of its three variances. The degrees of freedom of the test at each finite end of the set are in the df_limits attribute, and the df row holds those of the denominator's t. This inversion is the one the mratios function ttestratio() performs with iterativeCI = TRUE, which its documentation describes as searching iteratively for the limits by inverting the test; its default instead puts degrees of freedom computed at the estimate into Fieller's formula, and its documentation notes that those limits need not agree with the test. Hasler, Vonk, and Hothorn (2008) treat the three-arm design when the group variances differ.

The log ratio. ci_method = "log" forms the interval for \(\log \rho\) from the delta method standard error, \(\sqrt{v_{11}/\hat\theta_1^2 + v_{22}/\hat\theta_2^2 - 2 v_{12}/(\hat\theta_1 \hat\theta_2)}\), and maps it back by the exponential. This is the response ratio of meta-analysis (Hedges, Gurevitch, & Curtis, 1999), offered so a ratio reported here can be compared with one entered in a meta-analysis. It is defined only when both terms of the ratio are positive, and is refused otherwise with a condition of class dmar_log_ratio_undefined (which inherits dmar_refusal). It is always bounded; when the denominator is well determined it is close to Fieller's interval, and the two part company as the denominator's t falls. With unequal variances its degrees of freedom are the Satterthwaite degrees of freedom of the linearized log ratio.

The bootstrap. "percentile" and "bca" resample each group from itself (the baseline group too), as boot, the software of Davison and Hinkley (1997), does for several samples given as strata, and compute the ratio in every replication. The BCa interval reads its limits at quantile positions moved from those of the percentile interval by a bias correction, the median bias of the replications in normal units, and by an acceleration, the rate at which the standard error of the estimate changes with the parameter on a normalized scale (Efron & Tibshirani, 1993); its acceleration is estimated by the jackknife, deleting one observation at a time within its group, with each group's influence values scaled by its size. A bootstrap interval for a ratio is always bounded, whatever the denominator's t, so it can undercover badly when the denominator is near zero, exactly where Fieller's set becomes unbounded. When the Fieller set at the same level is unbounded, the line under the table says so. Pigeot et al. (2003) compare the percentile interval with Fieller's in the three-arm design. Summary statistics cannot be resampled, so a bootstrap from them is refused with a condition of class dmar_bootstrap_needs_data.

Bootstrap replications. The limits are quantiles of the B replicated ratios. A limit that cuts off a tail area \(\alpha\) is located by the replications beyond it, so the percentile interval is run only when B puts at least 10 replications beyond each limit asked for (400 with 0.025 in each tail; with unequal tail areas the smaller one decides, and a one-sided bound needs 10 beyond its one limit), and the BCa interval only with 50 beyond each nominal limit (2000 with 0.025 in each tail). A replication in which the ratio is undefined (a denominator of exactly zero, which discrete data can produce) is dropped and counted, never replaced, and the interval is computed from the rest. The result records B (requested), B_used (the number the interval rests on), n_dropped, and B_required (the fewest replications a request may ask for; that count is held to B, not to B_used) as attributes, and the line under the table states them, with bootstrap_status ("complete", "dropped", "exploratory", "insufficient_count", or "insufficient_share"). One warning of class dmar_bootstrap_replications_dropped states the counts when any replication was dropped, with a caution when the dropped replications are at least the 2.5 percent of B that lies beyond one limit at the 95 percent level, because they could then decide by themselves where that limit falls. When more than half were dropped, the limits asked for are NA, the estimate is returned, and the warning has class dmar_bootstrap_insufficient. For the BCa interval the count of 10 is applied again where the bias correction and the acceleration place the limits, and when fewer than 10 replications lie beyond one of them no BCa interval is reported (limits NA, the same class, with the two positions as positions and a suggested B as B_suggest). A BCa interval whose bias correction is infinite (every replicate on one side of the estimate) or whose jackknife is undefined (deleting one observation leaves a denominator of zero) stops with an error that names ci_method = "percentile". options(dmar.bootstrap_exploratory = TRUE) lets a smaller B (2 or more) run for a first look or a demonstration; every such call gives a warning of class dmar_bootstrap_exploratory and the result is not one to report. See dmar_bootstrap for the rule and its reasons.

Reading the interval for noninferiority. With a baseline, a new treatment is shown to retain more than a fraction \(f\) of the reference treatment's advantage, at one-sided level alpha_lower, exactly when \(f\) is below the lower limit of a set that is a bounded interval (or, for a one-sided bound, an interval unbounded only above) and whose denominator is positive. The one-sided bound is alpha_lower = 0.05, alpha_upper = 0, and a two-sided 95 percent interval gives the bound at one-sided level .025. Reporting the limit lets each reader apply his or her own fraction; the function itself tests no fraction and states no verdict. When the denominator is negative, or the set is unbounded below, the lower limit does not carry that reading.

References

Davison, A. C., & Hinkley, D. V. (1997). Bootstrap methods and their application. Cambridge University Press. doi:10.1017/CBO9780511802843

Efron, B., & Tibshirani, R. J. (1993). An introduction to the bootstrap. New York, NY: Chapman & Hall/CRC.

Fieller, E. C. (1941). The biological standardization of insulin. Supplement to the Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, 7(1), 1–54. doi:10.2307/2983630

Fieller, E. C. (1954). Some problems in interval estimation. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series B, 16(2), 175–185. doi:10.1111/j.2517-6161.1954.tb00159.x

Hasler, M., Vonk, R., & Hothorn, L. A. (2008). Assessing non-inferiority of a new treatment in a three-arm trial in the presence of heteroscedasticity. Statistics in Medicine, 27(4), 490–503. doi:10.1002/sim.3052

Hedges, L. V., Gurevitch, J., & Curtis, P. S. (1999). The meta-analysis of response ratios in experimental ecology. Ecology, 80(4), 1150–1156. doi:10.1890/0012-9658(1999)080[1150:TMAORR]2.0.CO;2

Pigeot, I., Schäfer, J., Röhmel, J., & Hauschke, D. (2003). Assessing non-inferiority of a new treatment in a three-arm clinical trial including a placebo. Statistics in Medicine, 22(6), 883–899. doi:10.1002/sim.1450

von Luxburg, U., & Franz, V. H. (2009). A geometric approach to confidence sets for ratios: Fieller's theorem, generalizations and bootstrap. Statistica Sinica, 19(3), 1095–1117.

See also

ci_ratio_of_means_paired for two means measured on the same units; summary_t_test and welch_t for the difference between two means.

Examples

# Drinks per week among the homeless alcohol-dependent adults of
# drinks_trial: the mean under the community reinforcement approach (CRA)
# relative to the mean under standard treatment. The group variances are
# not assumed equal.
drinks <- drinks_trial$drinks_per_week
cra <- drinks[drinks_trial$treatment == "CRA"]
standard <- drinks[drinks_trial$treatment == "Standard"]
ci_ratio_of_means(cra, standard)
#>  term           value 
#>  ci_lower       0.116 
#>  ratio          0.521 
#>  ci_upper       1.865 
#>  excluded_lower <NA>  
#>  excluded_upper <NA>  
#>  mean_1         26.636
#>  mean_2         51.110
#>  mean_baseline  <NA>  
#>  se_1           9.982 
#>  se_2           17.456
#>  se_baseline    <NA>  
#>  t_denominator  2.928 
#>  df             36    
#>  n_1            32    
#>  n_2            37    
#>  n_baseline     <NA>  
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%
#> 
#> Fieller confidence set: a bounded interval.

# The drinking counts are strongly skewed, so the response ratio interval
# and a BCa bootstrap interval are worth setting beside Fieller's;
# B = 2000 keeps the example quick, and a reported interval deserves the
# default B = 10000.
ci_ratio_of_means(cra, standard, ci_method = "log")
#>  term           value 
#>  ci_lower       0.189 
#>  ratio          0.521 
#>  ci_upper       1.435 
#>  excluded_lower <NA>  
#>  excluded_upper <NA>  
#>  mean_1         26.636
#>  mean_2         51.110
#>  mean_baseline  <NA>  
#>  se_1           9.982 
#>  se_2           17.456
#>  se_baseline    <NA>  
#>  t_denominator  2.928 
#>  df             36    
#>  n_1            32    
#>  n_2            37    
#>  n_baseline     <NA>  
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%
#> 
#> Log ratio interval: a bounded interval.
ci_ratio_of_means(cra, standard, ci_method = "bca", B = 2000, seed = 113)
#>  term           value 
#>  ci_lower       0.156 
#>  ratio          0.521 
#>  ci_upper       1.276 
#>  excluded_lower <NA>  
#>  excluded_upper <NA>  
#>  mean_1         26.636
#>  mean_2         51.110
#>  mean_baseline  <NA>  
#>  se_1           9.982 
#>  se_2           17.456
#>  se_baseline    <NA>  
#>  t_denominator  2.928 
#>  df             36    
#>  n_1            32    
#>  n_2            37    
#>  n_baseline     <NA>  
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%
#> 
#> BCa bootstrap interval: a bounded interval.
#> 
#> Bootstrap: 2000 replications, 2000 used (0 dropped; at least 2000 must be requested)

# From the summary statistics a paper reports, with pooled variances.
ci_ratio_of_means(mean_1 = 104, sd_1 = 14, n_1 = 40,
                  mean_2 = 96, sd_2 = 15, n_2 = 42, var_equal = TRUE)
#>  term           value  
#>  ci_lower       1.016  
#>  ratio          1.083  
#>  ci_upper       1.155  
#>  excluded_lower <NA>   
#>  excluded_upper <NA>   
#>  mean_1         104.000
#>  mean_2         96.000 
#>  mean_baseline  <NA>   
#>  se_1           2.296  
#>  se_2           2.241  
#>  se_baseline    <NA>

# A three-arm trial reported as summary statistics: the fraction of the
# reference arm's advantage over placebo that the new arm retains.
ci_ratio_of_means(mean_1 = 60.1, sd_1 = 12.2, n_1 = 60,
                  mean_2 = 62.4, sd_2 = 10.1, n_2 = 60,
                  mean_baseline = 50.3, sd_baseline = 9.8,
                  n_baseline = 60)
#>  term           value  
#>  ci_lower       0.512  
#>  ratio          0.810  
#>  ci_upper       1.171  
#>  excluded_lower <NA>   
#>  excluded_upper <NA>   
#>  mean_1         60.100 
#>  mean_2         62.400 
#>  mean_baseline  50.300 
#>  se_1           1.575  
#>  se_2           1.304  
#>  se_baseline    1.265  
#>  t_denominator  6.660  
#>  df             117.893
#>  n_1            60     
#>  n_2            60     
#>  n_baseline     60     
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%
#> 
#> Fieller confidence set: a bounded interval.

# A three-arm trial: the fraction of the reference treatment's advantage
# over placebo that a new treatment retains, with a one-sided 95 percent
# lower bound. Noninferiority at a retained fraction f holds for every f
# below the lower limit.
set.seed(113)
placebo <- rnorm(60, mean = 50, sd = 10)
reference <- rnorm(60, mean = 62, sd = 10)
new_drug <- rnorm(60, mean = 60, sd = 12)
ci_ratio_of_means(new_drug, reference, baseline = placebo,
                  alpha_lower = 0.05, alpha_upper = 0)
#>  term           value  
#>  ci_lower       0.357  
#>  ratio          0.678  
#>  ci_upper       Inf    
#>  excluded_lower <NA>   
#>  excluded_upper <NA>   
#>  mean_1         57.699 
#>  mean_2         60.465 
#>  mean_baseline  51.864 
#>  se_1           1.353  
#>  se_2           1.359  
#>  se_baseline    1.312  
#>  t_denominator  4.553  
#>  df             117.855
#>  n_1            60     
#>  n_2            60     
#>  n_baseline     60     
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95% (one-sided: the lower limit is the 95% lower confidence bound, with tail area 0.05 below it and none above the upper limit)
#> 
#> Fieller confidence set: an interval unbounded above.
